encoding: int8, each vector scaled by its own largest component, base64

items.title: Tokens
items.text: A language model does not read letters or whole words. Text is first cut into tokens, pieces drawn from a fixed vocabulary, and every token is replaced by an integer id.

items.title: Byte pair encoding
items.text: Byte pair encoding (BPE) builds a vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent pair of adjacent symbols. Common words end up as a single token, while rare words are spelled out from several pieces.

items.title: Token embeddings
items.text: The first layer of a language model is a lookup table with one learned vector per token id. Tokens that appear in similar contexts end up with similar vectors.

items.title: Position information
items.text: Self-attention by itself ignores the order of the tokens, so position information has to be injected. Older models add a learned vector per position; RoPE instead rotates queries and keys by an angle that grows with the position.

items.title: Self-attention
items.text: In self-attention every token builds a query, compares it with the keys of all tokens, and takes a weighted average of their values. The weights come from a softmax over the query-key dot products.

items.title: Transformer block
items.text: A transformer block is self-attention followed by a small feed-forward network, each wrapped in a residual connection and layer normalization. A modern language model stacks dozens of such blocks.

items.title: Next-token prediction
items.text: A GPT is trained on one task: predict the next token. A causal mask hides the future, so a single pass over a text gives a training signal at every position.

items.title: Temperature
items.text: A language model outputs a score, called a logit, for every token in its vocabulary. Dividing the logits by a temperature before the softmax makes sampling more random above 1 and more predictable below 1.

items.title: top_p and top_k
items.text: Nucleus sampling, the top_p setting, keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p and samples only among them. The top_k setting keeps a fixed number of candidates instead.

items.title: KV cache
items.text: While a model generates text, the keys and values computed for earlier tokens never change, so they are stored in a KV cache. Each new token then needs one pass for a single position instead of a pass over the whole prefix.

items.title: Context window
items.text: The context window is the largest number of tokens a model can take into account at once. Anything beyond it is cut off or has to be summarized, and memory use grows with every token that is kept.

items.title: Quantization
items.text: Quantization stores each weight with fewer bits, for example as an 8-bit or 4-bit integer instead of a 32-bit float. The file becomes several times smaller and inference faster, at the price of a small loss in accuracy.

items.title: GGUF
items.text: GGUF is the single-file format in which llama.cpp stores a model: the weights, the tokenizer and the settings needed to run it. Most GGUF files hold quantized weights, and the file name states the scheme.

items.title: Q4_K_M
items.text: Q4_K_M is a GGUF quantization preset that stores about 4 to 5 bits per weight. It is the usual default for running a model locally: about a third of the 16-bit size for a small loss in quality.

items.title: Q8_0
items.text: Q8_0 is a GGUF quantization preset that stores about 8 bits per weight. The file is roughly half the 16-bit size, and the output is almost indistinguishable from the original.

items.title: Q2_K
items.text: Q2_K is a GGUF quantization preset that stores about 3 bits per weight. It is the smallest of the common presets, and the loss in quality is plain to see.

items.title: LoRA
items.text: LoRA (low-rank adaptation) freezes the pretrained weights and learns a small update for chosen layers: the product of two thin matrices. Well under one percent of the parameters are trained, and the adapter can be merged into the weights afterwards.

items.title: Fine-tuning
items.text: Fine-tuning continues the training of a pretrained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset. It is good at changing tone, format or skill, and a poor way to store facts that change often.

items.title: Distillation
items.text: In knowledge distillation a compact student network is trained to reproduce the output probabilities of a much larger teacher. The student keeps most of the quality at a fraction of the cost.

items.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
items.text: Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, searches a document collection for passages related to the question and pastes them into the prompt. The model answers from that text, so its knowledge can be updated without retraining.

items.title: Chunking
items.text: Before documents are indexed they are cut into chunks of a few hundred tokens, often with some overlap. Chunks that are too large blur the match; chunks that are too small lose their context.

items.title: Sentence embeddings
items.text: A sentence embedding model turns a piece of text into one fixed-length vector, placed so that texts with similar meaning lie close together. Closeness is usually measured by cosine similarity.

items.title: all-MiniLM-L6-v2
items.text: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is a sentence embedding model with 6 transformer layers and about 23 million parameters. It outputs vectors with 384 dimensions and is fast enough to run on a CPU.

items.title: all-mpnet-base-v2
items.text: all-mpnet-base-v2 is a sentence embedding model with 12 transformer layers and about 110 million parameters. It outputs vectors with 768 dimensions and is slower but more accurate than the small models.

items.title: BM25
items.text: BM25 ranks documents by the query words they contain. A rare word counts for more than a common one, repeating a word brings diminishing returns, and long documents are penalized.

items.title: Hybrid search and RRF
items.text: Hybrid search runs keyword search and vector search side by side and merges the two rankings. Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) gives each document the sum of 1 / (k + rank) over the lists, with k usually set to 60.

items.title: Reranking
items.text: A reranker is a cross-encoder: it reads the question and one candidate passage together and outputs a relevance score. It is too slow for a whole collection, so it only reorders the top results of a faster first stage.

items.title: Exact search
items.text: Exact nearest-neighbor search compares the query with every stored vector. It always returns the true neighbors, but its cost grows in step with the size of the collection.

items.title: HNSW
items.text: HNSW (hierarchical navigable small world) is a graph index. Every vector is linked to a few close neighbors on several layers; a search enters at the sparse top layer and walks greedily toward the query, layer by layer.

items.title: HNSW: M
items.text: In HNSW the parameter M is the number of links kept per node. A larger M improves recall on hard data and makes the index larger and slower to build.

items.title: HNSW: efConstruction
items.text: In HNSW the parameter efConstruction is the length of the candidate list while the graph is being built. A larger value gives a better graph and a longer build; it does not change the size of the index.

items.title: HNSW: efSearch
items.text: In HNSW the parameter efSearch is the length of the candidate list during a query. A larger value raises recall and makes every search slower; it can be changed at any time without rebuilding.

items.title: IVF
items.text: An IVF (inverted file) index groups the vectors into cells with k-means and stores each vector in the list of its nearest centroid. A query scans only the nprobe closest cells instead of the whole collection.

items.title: Product quantization
items.text: Product quantization (PQ) cuts a vector into sub-vectors and replaces each piece with the id of its nearest codebook entry. A vector of several kilobytes shrinks to a few dozen bytes, and distances are estimated from small lookup tables.

items.title: Locality-sensitive hashing
items.text: Locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) draws random hyperplanes and records on which side of each one a vector falls. Vectors that point in similar directions tend to get the same bit pattern and land in the same bucket.

items.title: Diffusion models
items.text: A diffusion model learns to remove noise. Training images are corrupted with Gaussian noise in many small steps, and the network learns to predict the noise that was added so that the corruption can be undone.

items.title: Samplers
items.text: Image generation with a diffusion model starts from pure noise and denoises it step by step. Samplers such as DDIM take larger, deterministic steps and cut the count from a thousand to a few dozen.

items.title: Classifier-free guidance
items.text: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) runs the denoiser twice, with and without the text prompt, and exaggerates the difference between the two predictions. A higher guidance scale follows the prompt more closely and reduces variety.

items.title: Q-learning
items.text: Q-learning keeps one number for every state and action: the reward expected from there on. After each step the number moves toward the reward just received plus the discounted best value of the next state.

items.title: SARSA
items.text: SARSA updates toward the value of the action the agent actually takes next, exploratory moves included. Next to a cliff it therefore learns a longer, safer path than Q-learning.

items.title: Epsilon-greedy
items.text: An epsilon-greedy agent picks a random action with probability epsilon and the best known action otherwise. Without the random moves it would never discover an option better than its first success.

items.title: Dyna-Q
items.text: Dyna-Q records what each action did and uses this learned model of the world to replay imagined transitions. Every real step is followed by many planning updates, so far fewer real steps are needed.

items.title: A* search
items.text: A* search always expands the node with the lowest sum of the cost so far and a heuristic estimate of the cost still to go. If the heuristic never overestimates, the first path that reaches the goal is optimal.

items.title: AlphaZero
items.text: AlphaZero combines Monte Carlo tree search with a neural network that suggests moves and evaluates positions. It learns by playing against itself, using the search results as training targets for the network.

items.title: Model Context Protocol
items.text: The Model Context Protocol, MCP, is an open standard that connects AI applications to external tools and data. Client and server exchange JSON-RPC 2.0 messages: tools/list announces the available tools and tools/call runs one.

items.title: Tool calling
items.text: With tool calling a model replies with a structured request, a function name plus JSON arguments, instead of plain text. The application runs the function and sends the result back as a new message.

items.title: Agents
items.text: An agent runs a model in a loop: the model chooses an action, a tool carries it out, and the observation is appended to the context. The loop ends when the model decides that the task is done.

items.title: Backpropagation
items.text: Backpropagation applies the chain rule from the loss backwards through every layer. One backward pass yields the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight.

items.title: Adam
items.text: Adam keeps a running average of each weight's gradient and of its square, and divides the first by the square root of the second. Every weight thus gets its own step size.

items.title: Convolution
items.text: A convolutional layer slides a small filter across the image and computes the same weighted sum at every position. Early layers respond to edges, deeper layers to textures and parts of objects.

items.title: Batching
items.text: An inference server groups requests that arrive close together and pushes them through the model as one batch. Throughput rises sharply while each request waits a little longer.

items.title: Hallucination
items.text: A language model can state falsehoods fluently, because it produces likely text instead of looking facts up. Grounding answers in retrieved sources and asking for citations reduces the problem.

items.title: HTTP 429
items.text: An API that answers with HTTP 429 is saying that the client has exceeded its rate limit of requests or tokens per minute. The client should wait, as the Retry-After header suggests, and retry with exponential backoff.

items.title: HTTP 401
items.text: An API that answers with HTTP 401 is saying that the request carries no valid API key. Retrying will not help; the key or the Authorization header has to be fixed.

items.title: HTTP 400
items.text: An API that answers with HTTP 400 is saying that the request itself is invalid, for example because the prompt is longer than the context window. The request has to be changed before it is sent again.
